name: Python Tooling: Environments, Packaging and Quality
author: Recurse
subject: tools
description: venv and pip, pyproject.toml, packaging and publishing, ruff, mypy, pytest in depth, logging, config and CI.

lesson.intro: Writing Python is half the job. The other half is tooling: environments that do not break, dependencies that install the same everywhere, a package others can install, and formatting, linting, type checks and tests that run on every commit.
objectives: Create virtual environments and declare dependencies with a lock file
Lay out, build and publish a package with a src layout and entry points
Run ruff, black and mypy and act on their findings
Write pytest suites with fixtures, conftest, parametrize and mocks
Use logging, environment configuration, pre-commit and CI

sections.title: Virtual environments and pip, properly
sections.key: Give every project its own virtual environment in `.venv`, and install with `python -m pip` so packages land in the interpreter you are running.
sections.body:
"It works on my machine" usually means two machines have different packages installed. The fix is one **virtual environment** (venv) per project: a folder, usually `.venv`, with its own `python` and `site-packages`.

[[code]]

**Activating** only puts `.venv/bin` first on your PATH, so `python` and `pip` mean the venv's copies. Editors, scripts and Dockerfiles often skip activation and call `.venv/bin/python` directly.

[[visual]]

**uv**, a fast tool written in Rust, does the same jobs: `uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`. The ideas are identical, so learn both.

visual.title: Habits that prevent environment bugs
rows: A bare `pip` on your PATH can belong to a different Python
System Python refuses with **externally-managed-environment**; the fix is a venv
Venvs are disposable: delete one and recreate it from your dependency files
`pipx install ruff` or `uv tool install ruff`
Command-line tools each get their own hidden venv
Otherwise its imports and linting differ from what runs

sections.code:
python3 -m venv .venv  # once per project
source .venv/bin/activate
# Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
which python   # ends in .venv/bin/python
python -m pip install httpx
python -m pip list     # installed here
deactivate

# the same with uv
uv venv
uv pip install httpx
uv run python app.py

# a global tool in its own venv
pipx install ruff
sections.deeper:
A venv holds a `python` that points at a base interpreter plus its own `site-packages`. `python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"` prints the venv folder, and `python -m pip show httpx` shows a package's version, location and requirements.

Need several Python versions side by side? `uv python install 3.12` or pyenv provide them, and each venv stays tied to the version that created it.

The externally-managed check exists because Linux distributions and Homebrew use their Python for their own tools; installing into it can break the operating system.
sections.pitfall: Fixing "externally-managed-environment" with `--break-system-packages` or sudo. Create a venv for the project instead, or use pipx for a global tool.

check.question: Why prefer python -m pip install over pip install?
choices: It is the only way to install from PyPI
It installs packages faster
It installs into the interpreter you are running, not whichever pip is first on PATH
It installs packages globally for all users
check.explanation: python -m pip runs pip as a module of that exact python, so the package lands where your code will import it from. A bare pip can belong to another Python installation.

sections.title: Dependencies: pyproject.toml, requirements and lock files
sections.key: Declare version ranges in `pyproject.toml`; an application also commits a lock file pinning every package, so every install gets identical versions.
sections.body:
A teammate clones your project and the tests fail: they got httpx 1.0 where you have 0.28. Nobody changed the code; the dependencies moved.

**pyproject.toml** lists what your code **needs** as version ranges:

[[visual]]

Most packages use **semantic versioning**, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: a major bump may break your code, a minor one adds features, a patch fixes bugs. So ranges often stop below the next major.

Ranges alone are not reproducible: new releases keep appearing, including **transitive** dependencies (your dependencies' dependencies). A **lock file** pins every package, direct and transitive, to an exact version.

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

items.title: Library you publish
points: Ships no lock file, so it can coexist with other packages in someone else's environment

items.title: Application or service
points: Commits a lock file: `uv.lock`, `poetry.lock` or a pinned `requirements.txt`
CI, teammates and production install from it

sections.code:
$ cat pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "weather-cli"
version = "0.3.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.27,<1",
    "rich~=13.7",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = ["pytest>=8", "ruff", "mypy"]

$ uv lock    # pins every package: uv.lock
$ pip freeze > requirements.txt
$ uv lock --upgrade   # upgrade on purpose
sections.deeper:
`pip freeze` prints every installed package with its exact version (`httpx==0.28.1`, `anyio==4.6.2`, ...), which is why it is redirected into a pinned requirements file. pip-tools' `pip-compile` and Poetry produce lock files too.

Upgrades become deliberate: regenerate the lock, run the tests, commit. Bots such as Dependabot or Renovate open those upgrade pull requests for you, and `pip-audit` checks your pinned versions against known vulnerabilities.

Development tools (pytest, ruff, mypy) go in a separate group: an extra such as `dev` under `[project.optional-dependencies]`, or uv's `[dependency-groups]`.
sections.pitfall: Committing only loose ranges for an application. Every fresh install can pick up new versions deep in the dependency tree; commit a lock file and upgrade on purpose.

activity.title: Read a pyproject.toml
activity.prompt: tomllib (standard library since 3.11) parses TOML into dicts. Split each requirement into a name and a constraint with a small regex such as ([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)(.*), then print the lines described in the comment instead of the whole dict.

props.code:
import tomllib

PYPROJECT = """
[project]
name = "weather-cli"
version = "0.3.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = ["httpx>=0.27,<1", "rich~=13.7", "platformdirs"]

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = ["pytest>=8", "ruff", "mypy"]
"""

data = tomllib.loads(PYPROJECT)
# Print "NAME VERSION", then one line per runtime dependency:
#   NAME: CONSTRAINT   (or "NAME: any version" if there is no constraint)
# and finally the dev extras by name only: "dev: pytest, ruff, mypy"
print(data)
props.task: Print weather-cli 0.3.0, then httpx: >=0.27,<1, rich: ~=13.7, platformdirs: any version, and dev: pytest, ruff, mypy.
props.expectOutput:
weather-cli 0.3.0
httpx: >=0.27,<1
rich: ~=13.7
platformdirs: any version
dev: pytest, ruff, mypy

check.question: Which versions does the specifier rich~=13.7 allow?
choices: 13.7 or newer, below 14.0
Any version from 13.0 to 13.7
13.7 or newer, with no upper bound
Exactly 13.7
check.explanation: ~= is the compatible release operator: ~=13.7 means >=13.7 and ==13.*, so 13.9 is fine and 14.0 is not. ~=13.7.2 would mean >=13.7.2 and below 13.8.

sections.title: Project layout, packaging and publishing
sections.key: A src layout, a build backend and entry points make an installable package; rehearse on TestPyPI, because each version number can be uploaded only once.
sections.body:
Sooner or later your code must be installable: a CLI your team runs, or a library on PyPI.

[[visual]]

The **src layout** keeps the package under `src/`, off the import path, so tests import the **installed** package. A missing file fails your tests instead of a user's install.

Watch the two names: you pip install the **distribution name** `weather-cli` and import `weather_cli`. Import names cannot contain dashes.

[[visual 2]]

During development, `python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"` installs in **editable** mode with the dev extra, so code changes apply without reinstalling.

[[visual 3]]

A broken 0.3.0 cannot be replaced: release 0.3.1 and **yank** 0.3.0.

visual.title: pyproject.toml tables
rows: Names the **build backend**: hatchling, setuptools, flit-core, poetry-core or uv's

steps.label: Build with `uv build` or `python -m build`
steps.detail: A **wheel** (.whl, pip just unpacks it) and a **source distribution** (.tar.gz)

steps.label: Upload to **TestPyPI**
steps.detail: `uv publish` or `twine upload`, to the separate practice index

steps.label: Install from TestPyPI into a fresh venv and try the command
Upload the same files to PyPI
steps.detail: Use trusted publishing from CI, or an API token

sections.deeper:
**Trusted publishing** lets a CI workflow prove its identity to PyPI with a short-lived token, so no long-lived API token exists to leak.

The source distribution holds the source plus metadata and is used when no suitable wheel exists, for example on an unusual platform. A pure-Python wheel is named like `weather_cli-0.3.0-py3-none-any.whl`.

Any build backend works with pip, because pip reads `[build-system]` and asks that backend to build.
sections.pitfall: Running tests from a flat layout and never installing the package. Everything imports from the project folder, then the published wheel is missing a module.

check.question: You published weather-cli 0.3.0 with a bug. What do you do?
choices: Upload the fixed file as 0.3.0-fixed to the same version
Ask users to reinstall 0.3.0 with --force
Delete the release and upload a fixed file as 0.3.0
Release 0.3.1 with the fix, and yank 0.3.0 if it is harmful
check.explanation: PyPI never lets you reuse a version number, even after deleting it, so caches and lock files can trust that a version always means the same files. Yanking hides a release from new installs without breaking existing pins.

sections.title: Formatting and linting with ruff and black
sections.key: A formatter rewrites code into one style so reviews skip spacing debates; a linter reads code without running it and reports likely bugs by rule code.
sections.body:
Review time spent on spacing, quotes and import order is wasted, and the arguments never end. Teams hand those choices to tools.

[[visual]]

Ruff groups its rules by prefix. You pick groups in `pyproject.toml` with `select = ["E", "F", "I", "B", "UP", "SIM"]` under `[tool.ruff.lint]`:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

`ruff check --fix .` applies the safe fixes. To silence one rule on one line, write `# noqa: E722` with a reason, never a bare `# noqa`.

Run the tools on save, in pre-commit, and in CI with check-only flags: `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .`.

items.title: Formatter
points: Rewrites layout into one consistent style
Black has almost no options, so there is nothing to debate
`ruff format` matches Black's output, much faster

items.title: Linter
points: Reports likely bugs and bad patterns
Ruff reimplements flake8, isort, pyupgrade, bugbear and more

visual.title: Ruff rule groups
rows: Real bugs: unused imports, undefined names
Old syntax for your Python version

sections.code:
import os, sys    # E401, F401 x2 (unused)
import json

def load(path, cache={}):  # B006
    if path in cache: return cache[path]
    # ^ E701: two statements on one line
    f = open(path)   # SIM115: use with
    data = json.load(f)
    cache[path] = data
    return data

def check(x):
    if x == None:    # E711: use is None
        return False
    try:
        return int(x) > 0
    except:          # E722: bare except
        return False

# ruff check: Found 9 errors (+ I001)
sections.deeper:
Each finding shows a location, a code and a message, such as `messy.py:1:8: F401 [*] os imported but unused`. A `[*]` marks findings that `--fix` repairs safely; unsafe fixes need `--unsafe-fixes`.

Ruff's default rule set has changed between versions, so list the groups you want explicitly instead of relying on defaults.

The F group deserves special respect: an unused import or an undefined name is often a real bug, not a style choice.
sections.pitfall: Sprinkling bare `# noqa` comments to quiet the linter. They hide every rule on that line, including future real bugs; fix the code, or silence one named rule.

check.question: What is the difference between a formatter and a linter?
choices: A formatter runs tests and a linter compiles code
A formatter rewrites layout into one consistent style; a linter reports likely bugs and bad patterns
They are two names for the same tool
A linter changes code automatically and a formatter only warns
check.explanation: black and ruff format change whitespace, quotes and line breaks without changing behavior. ruff check finds problems like unused imports or bare excepts, some of which it can also fix.

sections.title: Type checking with mypy
sections.key: mypy checks code against its type hints before it runs, but by default it skips the body of any function that has no annotations at all.
sections.body:
A function can return None and a caller forgets: in production that is `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'total_cents'`. **mypy** finds it in your editor first.

[[code]]

Typing is **gradual**: mypy reasons only about what is annotated, so `total()` passed silently. Enable `check_untyped_defs`, or set `strict = true` under `[tool.mypy]` for new projects; strict also requires annotations on every function.

[[visual]]

**Pyright**, which runs inside VS Code's Pylance, is the other major checker. Many teams use Pyright in the editor and mypy in CI.

visual.title: Everyday mypy
rows: Add `reveal_type(expr)`: mypy prints the type it inferred. Remove it after
`# type: ignore[union-attr]` with the code, so other errors still show
Add the stub package `types-PyYAML` as a dev dependency
Ship a `py.typed` file so users get your hints

sections.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Order:
    id: int
    total_cents: int

def find(orders: list[Order],
         oid: int) -> Order | None:
    for order in orders:
        if order.id == oid:
            return order
    return None

def label(oid: int) -> str:
    return "Order #" + oid   # str + int

def total(items):            # no hints
    return sum(items) + "x"  # not checked

o = find([Order(1, 500)], 1)
print(o.total_cents)         # o may be None

# $ mypy orders.py
# orders.py:16: error: Unsupported operand
#   types for + ("str" and "int")
#   [operator]
# orders.py:22: error: Item "None" of
#   "Order | None" has no attribute
#   "total_cents"  [union-attr]
sections.deeper:
Each mypy error names a file, a line, a message and an error code in brackets. The code is what goes into a targeted `# type: ignore[...]`.

With `strict = true`, the same file also reports `Function is missing a type annotation [no-untyped-def]` for `total()` and flags functions that return `Any` where a type was promised.

Third-party libraries either ship their own hints (marked by a `py.typed` file) or have separate stub packages named `types-...`.
sections.pitfall: Assuming a clean mypy run means the code is checked. Unannotated functions are skipped by default; enable `check_untyped_defs` or strict, and annotate as you go.

check.question: mypy reports nothing for def total(items): return sum(items) + "x". Why?
choices: mypy only checks code that has already run once
The code is actually correct
mypy only checks files named test_*.py
The function has no annotations, so by default mypy does not check its body
check.explanation: Gradual typing means unannotated code is left alone unless you turn on check_untyped_defs or strict. Adding a signature such as (items: list[int]) -> int makes mypy check the body and report the str + int problem.

sections.title: pytest in depth: fixtures, conftest and markers
sections.key: A fixture builds what a test needs and cleans up after its `yield`; the default function scope gives every test a fresh copy.
sections.body:
In a real codebase the test suite is a program of its own. **Fixtures** keep it fast, isolated and readable.

A fixture is a function marked `@pytest.fixture`. A test asks for one by naming it as a parameter, and fixtures can request other fixtures. Code after `yield` is teardown: it runs when the test ends, pass or fail.

[[code]]

**Scope** sets how often a fixture is built:

[[visual]]

**conftest.py** holds fixtures shared by every test in its folder and below. pytest discovers it automatically; you never import it.

[[visual 2]]

items.title: function
points: A fresh fixture for every test
No test can see another's changes

items.title: module, package, session
points: For expensive, read-only resources such as a database container
Mutate it and tests start depending on their order

visual.title: Built-in fixtures and everyday flags
rows: Temporarily replaces attributes, environment variables or dict entries
Open the debugger at the failing line

sections.code:
# tests/conftest.py
@pytest.fixture
def inventory():
    inv = Inventory()   # fresh per test
    inv.add("pen", 10)
    return inv

@pytest.fixture
def db(tmp_path):   # uses another fixture
    conn = sqlite3.connect(tmp_path / "db")
    yield conn     # the test runs here
    conn.close()   # teardown, pass or fail

# tests/test_inventory.py
def test_remove(inventory):
    inventory.remove("pen", 3)
    assert inventory.count("pen") == 7

def test_fresh_copy(inventory):
    # the removal above is gone
    assert inventory.count("pen") == 10
sections.deeper:
**Markers** label tests: `@pytest.mark.skip`, `@pytest.mark.skipif(sys.platform == "win32", reason=...)`, `@pytest.mark.xfail` for a known bug, or your own such as `@pytest.mark.slow`. Register custom markers in `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` and deselect them with `pytest -m "not slow"`.

Fixture chains are common in web projects: a `client` fixture depends on an `app` fixture, which depends on a `database` fixture. pytest builds each once per scope and tears them down in reverse order.
sections.pitfall: Sharing a mutable object through a session-scoped fixture. One test changes it, and others pass or fail depending on run order; keep wide-scope fixtures read-only.

check.question: Two tests both request the inventory fixture, which has the default scope. The first test removes 3 pens. What does the second test see?
choices: An error, because a fixture can be used only once
7 pens, because fixtures are shared
10 pens, because each test gets a fresh inventory
It depends on which test runs first
check.explanation: Function scope means the fixture function runs again for every test, so changes never leak between tests. That isolation is why it is the default.

sections.title: Parametrize and mocking in practice
sections.key: Parametrize runs one test body per row of inputs; a mock stands in for a slow or risky collaborator, patched where the code under test looks it up.
sections.body:
Most functions need many input cases, and interesting code talks to slow or risky things: email, payments, the clock.

**Parametrize** turns one test into a table. Each row is reported as its own test, so one failure does not hide the others. Stacked decorators multiply: 3 rows times 2 rows is 6 tests.

[[code]]

A **Mock** accepts any call and records it:

[[visual]]

Patch the name **where it is looked up**. shipping.py did `from emails import send_email`, so shipping holds its own reference:

[[visual 2]]

Mock at the boundaries of your system, not every internal function, or tests break on every refactor.

visual.title: Configuring and checking a Mock
rows: Fails unless exactly one call had those arguments
Real signature: wrong arguments fail. Also `autospec=True`

visual.title: Which target to patch
rows: Replaces the name shipping calls: the fake is used
Changes only emails: shipping still calls the real function

sections.code:
@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ("weight", "express", "expected"),
    [
        (0.5, False, 5.0),
        (2.0, True, 16.0),
        pytest.param(1.0, True, 10.0,
                     id="boundary"),
    ],
)
def test_cost(weight, express, expected):
    got = shipping_cost(weight, express)
    assert got == expected

def test_notify_sends_email(monkeypatch):
    sent = Mock()
    monkeypatch.setattr(
        "shipping.send_email", sent)
    to = "ana@example.com"
    assert notify_shipped(to, 42)
    sent.assert_called_once_with(
        to, "Order 42 has shipped")
sections.deeper:
`patch(...)` works as a decorator or a context manager, and `monkeypatch.setattr(...)` is pytest's equivalent; both restore the original after the test. The pytest-mock plugin wraps the same API in a `mocker` fixture.

Parametrize rows can carry readable names with `pytest.param(..., id="boundary-express")` or an `ids=` list, and marks such as `marks=pytest.mark.xfail` for one known-bad row.

`monkeypatch.setenv("API_KEY", "test")` and `monkeypatch.delenv(...)` are the clean way to test configuration code.
sections.pitfall: Patching the name where it is defined instead of where it is used. If shipping.py did `from emails import send_email`, patch `shipping.send_email`.

activity.title: Mock a flaky payment gateway
activity.prompt: Mock() accepts any call. Set gateway.charge.return_value for the first case. For the others, create a new Mock and set gateway.charge.side_effect to a list [ConnectionError(), {"id": "r2"}] or to a single exception, then print the result and gateway.charge.call_count.

props.code:
from unittest.mock import Mock

def charge(gateway, amount_cents):
    """Charge once, retry once on ConnectionError, return the receipt id or None."""
    for attempt in range(2):
        try:
            return gateway.charge(amount_cents)["id"]
        except ConnectionError:
            continue
    return None

gateway = Mock()
# 1. Make gateway.charge return {"id": "r1"}; print charge(gateway, 500).
# 2. New Mock: fail once, then return {"id": "r2"}; print the result and charge.call_count.
# 3. New Mock: always raise ConnectionError; print the result and charge.call_count.
print(gateway.charge(500))   # an unconfigured Mock returns another Mock
props.task: Print r1, then r2 2, then None 2.

check.question: shipping.py does from emails import send_email. Which target makes a test's fake replace the call inside shipping?
choices: patch("emails.send_email")
patch("shipping.send_email")
patch("send_email")
patch("emails")
check.explanation: The import created a name send_email inside the shipping module, and that is the name notify_shipped looks up. Patching emails.send_email replaces a different reference.

sections.title: Logging instead of print
sections.key: Log with a per-module logger and levels, configure logging once at the entry point, and remember unconfigured Python shows only WARNING and above.
sections.body:
At 2 a.m. the import job fails. Prints give no timestamps, no severity and no clue which module spoke. The `logging` module fixes that.

[[visual]]

- Every module: `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)`. Loggers form a tree by dotted name.
- Configure **once**, at the entry point. **Libraries never configure logging**; the application decides what shows.
- Pass values as arguments: `logger.info("imported %d rows", n)`. Formatting is skipped when the level is off, and log tools group messages by template.
- In an `except` block, `logger.exception(...)` logs ERROR plus the traceback.

[[code]]

Never log passwords, tokens or card numbers.

visual.title: Levels, least to most severe
rows: Something odd, but the program carries on. The default threshold

sections.code:
import logging
import sys

# one logger per module
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
fmt = "%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s"

def import_rows(rows):
    ok = 0
    for n, row in enumerate(rows, start=1):
        if row.get("qty", "").isdigit():
            ok += 1
        else:
            logger.warning("bad row %d", n)
    logger.info("rows imported: %d", ok)

def main():  # the entry point configures
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
                        stream=sys.stdout,
                        format=fmt)
    import_rows([{"qty": "3"}, {"qty": ""}])
    logger.debug("hidden: below INFO")

main()
# WARNING __main__: bad row 2
# INFO __main__: rows imported: 1
sections.deeper:
`logging.basicConfig(...)` suits simple programs; `logging.config.dictConfig` sets up several handlers (console, file, a log service) and formatters. Because loggers form a tree (`app.db` sits under `app`), you can turn on DEBUG for one package without touching code.

Production systems usually emit **structured logs**: one JSON object per line with fields such as level, logger, message, request id and user id, so a log platform can search and filter them. A JSON formatter or structlog does this without changing your logging calls.

Logs are copied to many places and kept for a long time, which is why secrets and needless personal data must stay out.
sections.pitfall: Calling `logging.basicConfig` inside a library or in many modules. Only the first call takes effect; configure once, at the application's entry point.

activity.title: Replace prints with log calls
activity.prompt: Swap each print for logger.warning, logger.info or logger.debug, passing values as arguments ("charging %s %d", customer, cents). The basicConfig line is already set to INFO, so the debug message should disappear.

props.code:
import logging
import sys

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
                    stream=sys.stdout, force=True)   # force: replace handlers from earlier runs
logger = logging.getLogger("billing")

def charge(customer, cents):
    if cents <= 0:
        print("refusing charge for", customer)       # should be a WARNING
        return False
    print("charging", customer, cents)               # should be INFO
    print("card token tok_123")                      # DEBUG: must not show at INFO level
    return True

charge("ana", 500)
charge("bo", 0)
props.task: Print exactly two lines: INFO billing: charging ana 500 and WARNING billing: refusing charge for bo.
props.expectOutput:
INFO billing: charging ana 500
WARNING billing: refusing charge for bo

check.question: A module calls logger.info("started"), but nothing appears, and the program never configures logging. Why?
choices: Without configuration, only WARNING and above are shown
getLogger(__name__) creates a disabled logger
print and logging cannot be used in the same program
info messages are always discarded
check.explanation: The root logger defaults to WARNING, and the fallback handler prints only warnings and errors. Calling basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) at the entry point makes info messages appear.

sections.title: Configuration with environment variables
sections.key: Read configuration from environment variables once at startup into a typed object, fail fast if anything is missing, and convert values, because each one is a string.
sections.body:
The same code runs on your laptop, in CI and in production, but the database, keys and debug switch differ. Hard-coding them means editing code per environment and, sooner or later, committing a secret. The **twelve-factor** approach keeps configuration in **environment variables**, set by your shell, Docker Compose, CI or the host.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Locally, keep variables in a `.env` file loaded by python-dotenv or `uv run --env-file .env`. Add `.env` to `.gitignore` and commit a `.env.example` with fake values. In production, a secret manager or the platform injects the real values.

visual.title: A solid configuration pattern
rows: Read once at startup into a frozen dataclass or a pydantic-settings model
No `os.environ` calls scattered through the code
**Fail fast** on a missing or bad value
A clear error at deploy time beats a failure on some request an hour later
Every environment value is a string
`bool("false")` is True: any non-empty string is truthy
A missing DATABASE_URL must not silently point at a dev database

sections.tip: Take the environment as a parameter, `load_settings(env=os.environ)`, and tests can pass a plain dict or use `monkeypatch.setenv`.
sections.pitfall: Reading booleans with `bool(os.environ.get("DEBUG"))`. Any non-empty string, including "false" and "0", is True, so debug turns on in production.

activity.title: Parse settings from the environment
activity.prompt: Run it first and spot the bugs: port is None, "false" becomes True and hosts is one string. Convert PORT with int() and a default of "8000", treat only 1, true, yes or on (any case) as True, and split ALLOWED_HOSTS on commas, stripping spaces and dropping empty names.

props.code:
def load(env):
    """Return {"port": int (default 8000), "debug": bool (default False),
    "hosts": list of names from a comma-separated ALLOWED_HOSTS (default [])}."""
    return {
        "port": env.get("PORT"),
        "debug": bool(env.get("DEBUG")),
        "hosts": env.get("ALLOWED_HOSTS"),
    }

print(load({}))
print(load({"PORT": "9000", "DEBUG": "false", "ALLOWED_HOSTS": "example.com, api.example.com"}))
print(load({"DEBUG": "TRUE"}))
props.task: Print {'port': 8000, 'debug': False, 'hosts': []}, then {'port': 9000, 'debug': False, 'hosts': ['example.com', 'api.example.com']}, then {'port': 8000, 'debug': True, 'hosts': []}.

check.question: Where should a production database password live?
choices: In the .env.example file
In settings.py, committed to the repository
In an environment variable injected by a secret manager or the hosting platform
In a comment in the README
check.explanation: Secrets stay out of the code and the repository; the platform injects them at runtime. .env.example holds placeholder values only, so people know which variables to set.

sections.title: pre-commit hooks and CI for Python
sections.key: pre-commit runs checks on staged files before each commit, but hooks can be skipped, so CI running the same checks on every pull request is the real gate.
sections.body:
Formatters, linters, type checkers and tests only help if they run every time, for everyone.

[[visual]]

**pre-commit** reads `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, with each hook pinned to a release tag (`rev`). Run `pre-commit install` once per clone. `pre-commit run --all-files` checks the whole repository, and `pre-commit autoupdate` bumps the pins.

Anyone can skip hooks with `git commit --no-verify`, or never install them, so **CI is the source of truth**:

[[code]]

A **matrix** runs the job once per listed Python version, in parallel. **Branch protection** on main then requires the checks to pass before merging.

steps.label: `git commit`
steps.detail: pre-commit runs ruff, ruff-format and mypy on the staged files

steps.label: Did a hook fail or rewrite a file?
steps.yes: The commit stops: look, stage again, commit

steps.label: Push and open a pull request
CI runs on every push and pull request
steps.detail: Check out, set up Python, install from the lock file, ruff and mypy, then tests with coverage

steps.label: Branch protection allows the merge only when checks pass

sections.code:
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
    rev: v0.17.0
    hooks:
      - id: ruff
        args: [--fix]
      - id: ruff-format

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v6
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
          cache: pip
      - run: python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
      - run: ruff check .
      - run: ruff format --check .
      - run: mypy src
      - run: pytest --cov=weather_cli
sections.deeper:
Put the fast checks (ruff, mypy) before the slow ones (tests), so a typo fails in seconds. Cache downloaded packages between runs (`cache: pip`).

A matrix matters most for libraries that promise support for several Python versions or operating systems. Keep CI to a few minutes: slow pipelines tempt people to batch changes into huge pull requests.

A release workflow can build the package and publish it with trusted publishing when you push a version tag. Shipping Code: CI/CD and the Cloud walks through workflow syntax line by line.
sections.pitfall: Relying on pre-commit hooks as the only gate. They can be skipped or never installed; run the same checks in CI and require them before merging.

check.question: Your team uses pre-commit hooks. Why run the same checks again in CI?
choices: Hooks can be skipped or never installed, so only CI guarantees every merged change was checked
pre-commit cannot run mypy
GitHub requires it
CI runs them faster
check.explanation: pre-commit gives fast local feedback, but it depends on each developer's setup. CI plus branch protection is the gate nobody can forget.

keyTerms.definition: A per-project folder with its own Python and site-packages, so projects cannot break each other's dependencies.
The standard file for a Python project's metadata, dependencies, build backend and tool configuration.
A file pinning every direct and transitive dependency to an exact version, so every install is identical.
A package your dependencies depend on, installed even though you never listed it.
A version specifier such as ~=13.7, meaning at least 13.7 and below 14.0.
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbering where major bumps may break callers, minor bumps add features and patch bumps fix bugs.
A project structure with the package under src/, so tests run against the installed package.
A built Python package archive (.whl) that pip installs by unpacking, without running build steps.
pip install -e: installs a project so imports point at its source folder and edits apply immediately.
A tool such as ruff that reads code without running it and reports likely bugs and style problems.
A tool such as mypy or Pyright that checks type hints statically and reports code that cannot work with them.
A function marked @pytest.fixture that builds test setup; tests request it by parameter name, and code after yield is teardown.
A file pytest discovers automatically that holds fixtures and hooks shared by the tests in its folder.
A stand-in object that records how it is called and returns configured values, used to replace slow or risky collaborators in tests.
Keeping deployment-specific configuration such as URLs and secrets in environment variables rather than in code.
A check that runs automatically on staged files before git creates a commit.

summary: One venv per project, `python -m pip`, never `sudo pip`.
Ranges in pyproject.toml; applications also commit a lock file.
src layout, build backend, entry points; rehearse on TestPyPI.
ruff and black end style debates; mypy skips unannotated code unless strict.
Fixtures with yield, narrow scopes, parametrize and boundary mocks.
Log with levels, read config once from the environment, gate merges in CI.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new teammate why the project has both a pyproject.toml and a lock file, what each one is for, and what would go wrong if you deleted the lock file.

questions.question: pip install requests fails with "error: externally-managed-environment". What is the right fix?
choices: Download the package by hand and copy it into site-packages
Run it again with sudo
Add --break-system-packages
Create and activate a virtual environment for the project, then install there
questions.explanation: The system Python belongs to the operating system, so pip refuses to change it. A venv gives the project its own site-packages. sudo and --break-system-packages override the protection and can break system tools.

questions.question: Create a virtual environment in a folder named .venv in the current directory, using python3.
questions.explanation: The standard library's venv module creates the folder with its own interpreter link and site-packages. uv venv does the same thing faster if you use uv.

questions.question: What does running source .venv/bin/activate actually change?
choices: It copies the packages into the system Python
It puts .venv/bin first on your PATH, so python and pip refer to the venv's copies
It starts a new Python process that stays running
It is required before .venv/bin/python can import anything
questions.explanation: Activation is a convenience that edits PATH and the prompt in your shell. Calling .venv/bin/python directly uses the venv without activating, which is how scripts and Dockerfiles usually do it.

questions.question: Which of these belong in your git repository? Select all that apply.
choices: pyproject.toml
The lock file (uv.lock or a pinned requirements.txt)
The .venv folder
A .env file with real API keys
.env.example with placeholder values
__pycache__ folders
questions.explanation: Commit what lets someone rebuild the project: the dependency declaration, the lock file and an example config. Environments and caches are machine-specific and rebuildable, and real secrets never go in git.

questions.question: Which pip subcommand prints every installed package with its exact version, in a form you can redirect into requirements.txt?
questions.explanation: pip freeze lists name==version for everything in the environment, including transitive dependencies, which makes a simple lock file. pip list shows the same packages in a table that pip cannot install from.

questions.question: You are publishing a library on PyPI that uses httpx. How should its pyproject.toml declare that dependency?
choices: Vendor a copy of httpx inside the library
httpx==0.28.1, pinned exactly
httpx with no version at all, always
A range such as httpx>=0.27,<1, with no lock file shipped
questions.explanation: A library is installed next to other packages, and an exact pin would conflict with anyone who needs a different patch release. Applications pin exactly in a lock file; libraries declare the range they support.

questions.question: What is a transitive dependency, and why does it make lock files necessary?
questions.answer: A dependency of one of your dependencies. Your ranges do not pin them, so a fresh install can pick up a new version deep in the tree; a lock file pins every package exactly so all installs match.
questions.explanation: Many surprise breakages come from a package you never listed. Locking everything and upgrading on purpose, with tests, turns those surprises into reviewed changes.

questions.question: In semantic versioning, which part of 4.2.7 changes for a release that may break existing code? Answer with the word.
questions.explanation: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking changes bump the major number (4 to 5), new features bump the minor, and bug fixes bump the patch.

questions.question: Put the steps of a first release in order.
items: Build the sdist and wheel with uv build or python -m build
Install from TestPyPI into a fresh venv and try it
Upload the same files to PyPI
questions.explanation: TestPyPI is a dress rehearsal: the fresh-venv install proves the package works for someone who does not have your source folder. Only then publish the identical files for real.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of the src layout?
choices: It lets you skip writing pyproject.toml
It makes imports faster at runtime
Tests import the installed package, so packaging mistakes fail in your tests instead of for users
It is required by PyPI
questions.explanation: With the package under src/, it is not importable from the project root by accident. You must install it (usually editable), which exercises the same packaging users get.

questions.question: Match each file or setting with its job.

pairs.right: Project metadata, dependencies and tool configuration
Marks a folder as an importable package
Runs when you type python -m package_name
Declares console commands created at install time
A built archive that pip installs by unpacking
Names the backend that builds the package

questions.explanation: These six pieces cover nearly every modern Python package, whichever build backend you choose.

questions.question: Install the project in the current folder in editable mode, together with its dev extra, using pip through the interpreter.
questions.explanation: -e (editable) links the installed package to your source folder, and .[dev] means this project plus its dev optional dependencies. The quotes stop shells such as zsh from treating the brackets as a pattern.

questions.question: Which ruff rule code, from the Pyflakes (F) group, flags an import that is never used?
questions.explanation: F rules come from Pyflakes and catch real mistakes. F401 is "imported but unused", and ruff check --fix can remove the import automatically.

questions.question: With select = ["E", "F", "B"] in the ruff config, which problems in this code are reported? Select all that apply.
choices: os is imported but unused (F401)
b == None should use is None (E711)
The bare except: (E722)
The mutable default seen=[] (B006)
The function has no docstring
The function has no type hints
questions.explanation: All four are reported with those groups selected. Docstrings and type hints are checked only by other rule groups (D and ANN), which this configuration does not enable.

questions.question: In CI, check that every file is already formatted, without changing any file, using ruff on the current folder.
questions.explanation: --check reports files that would be reformatted and exits non-zero, failing the build, while leaving files untouched. Locally you run ruff format . to apply the changes.

questions.question: Why do teams adopt an opinionated formatter such as Black or ruff format?
choices: It is required to publish on PyPI
It ends style debates in review, and every file looks the same
It finds logic bugs in the code
It makes the code run faster
questions.explanation: With formatting automated, diffs only show real changes, and reviewers spend their attention on behavior and design. Finding bugs is the linter's job.

questions.question: mypy says: Library stubs not installed for "yaml". Which package do you add as a dev dependency? Use the name pip installs.
questions.explanation: Libraries without built-in hints get community stubs on PyPI named types-<distribution>. PyYAML's are types-PyYAML. Libraries that ship a py.typed file need nothing extra.

questions.question: Which way of silencing one mypy error is best when you really must?
choices: # type: ignore[union-attr]
Annotating the variable as Any
Deleting the type hints from the function
# type: ignore
questions.explanation: A coded ignore silences only that error on that line, so a new, different mistake there is still reported. A bare ignore or Any hides everything.

questions.question: Complete the configuration so mypy requires annotations everywhere and enables its strictest checks.
choices: warn_unused_ignores
ignore_missing_imports
strict
follow_imports
questions.explanation: strict turns on a bundle of flags, including disallow_untyped_defs and check_untyped_defs. ignore_missing_imports does the opposite of tightening: it silences missing-module errors.

questions.question: What does reveal_type(x) do, and when do you use it?
questions.answer: When mypy checks the file, it prints the type it inferred for x. Use it to understand a confusing error, then remove it.
questions.explanation: Many confusing errors come from an inferred type you did not expect, such as int | None after a dict.get(). Seeing the inferred type points straight at the missing check.

questions.question: Complete the fixture so the connection is closed after each test, even when the test fails.
choices: yield
await
raise
return
questions.explanation: Code after yield is teardown, and pytest runs it after the test finishes, pass or fail. With return, the close() line would never run.

questions.question: These tests pass alone but fail when run together in a different order. What is wrong?
choices: assert cannot compare lists
Session fixtures cannot return lists
The tests need the @pytest.mark.order marker
The session-scoped list is shared and mutated, so each test sees what earlier tests did; use function scope
questions.explanation: A session fixture is created once and the same list is handed to every test. test_add_item leaves "pen" in it, so whichever test runs second fails. Function scope gives each test its own list.

questions.question: What is conftest.py for?
choices: Configuring Python's import path for production code
Holding fixtures (and hooks) shared by every test in its folder and below, discovered automatically
Listing which tests to skip
Storing test data files
questions.explanation: pytest loads conftest.py files on its own, so fixtures defined there are available to tests without imports. Put widely used fixtures in the top-level tests/conftest.py.

questions.question: Rerun only the tests that failed in the previous pytest run.
questions.explanation: --lf (last failed) uses pytest's cache of the previous run. --ff runs the failures first and then everything else.

questions.question: A test has @pytest.mark.parametrize with 3 rows stacked on another @pytest.mark.parametrize with 2 rows. How many tests does pytest collect?
questions.explanation: Stacked parametrize decorators produce every combination of their rows: 3 times 2 is 6 test cases.

questions.question: m = Mock(); m.side_effect = [ConnectionError(), "ok"]. What happens on the first and second calls to m()?
choices: Both calls return the list
Both calls raise ConnectionError
The first returns ConnectionError as a value; the second returns "ok"
The first call raises ConnectionError; the second returns "ok"
questions.explanation: A list (any iterable) as side_effect is consumed one item per call: exception instances are raised and other values are returned. A third call would raise StopIteration.

questions.question: This test sends a real email. Why?
questions.code:
# shipping.py
from emails import send_email
def notify_shipped(email, order_id):
    send_email(email, f"Order {order_id} has shipped")

# test_shipping.py
from unittest.mock import patch
from shipping import notify_shipped

def test_notify():
    with patch("emails.send_email") as fake:
        notify_shipped("a@example.com", 1)
        fake.assert_called_once()
choices: patch only works as a decorator
The with block exits before notify_shipped runs
shipping holds its own reference to send_email, so patching emails.send_email does not affect it
assert_called_once sends the email
questions.explanation: from emails import send_email copies the reference into shipping's namespace when shipping is imported. Patch shipping.send_email instead, or have shipping do import emails and call emails.send_email.

questions.question: Complete the assertion so the test checks the mock was called exactly once with these arguments.
questions.code:
sent = Mock()
notify_shipped("ana@example.com", order_id=42, send=sent)
sent._____("ana@example.com", "Order 42 has shipped")
choices: assert_any_call_once
assert_called_once_with
called_with
return_value
questions.explanation: assert_called_once_with fails unless there was exactly one call with exactly these arguments. called_with and assert_any_call_once are not real methods: Python 3.12 and later raise AttributeError for such near-miss names, and older versions silently created a new attribute that checked nothing.

questions.question: Why write logger.info("loaded %d rows", n) instead of logger.info(f"loaded {n} rows")?
choices: Formatting is skipped when INFO is disabled, and log tools can group messages that share a template
%d rounds the number
It makes the message appear at a higher level
f-strings are not allowed in log calls
questions.explanation: logging only merges the arguments into the message if a handler will emit it. The constant template also lets aggregation tools count every "loaded %d rows" together. The f-string version works, it is just less efficient and less searchable.

questions.question: Put the logging levels in order from least to most severe.
questions.explanation: Setting a level shows that level and everything more severe. With level=WARNING you see WARNING, ERROR and CRITICAL.

questions.question: You are writing a reusable library. Which logging practices are right? Select all that apply.
choices: Create loggers with logging.getLogger(__name__)
Call logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) on import
Use logger.exception inside except blocks that handle an error
Log the user's password on failed logins to help debugging
Let the application decide which levels are shown
questions.explanation: Libraries log and leave configuration to the application. Configuring on import overrides the application's setup, and passwords must never be written to logs.

questions.question: What does print(bool("false")) output?
questions.explanation: bool() of any non-empty string is True. Environment variables are always strings, so booleans need explicit parsing such as value.lower() in ("1", "true", "yes", "on").

questions.question: This crashes with TypeError at startup. What is the bug?
questions.code:
import os
port = os.environ.get("PORT", "8000")
next_port = port + 1
choices: os.environ.get cannot take a default
PORT must be lowercase
Environment values are strings; convert with int() before adding
8000 is not a valid port
questions.explanation: "8000" + 1 mixes a str and an int. int(os.environ.get("PORT", "8000")) converts once, at the point where configuration is loaded.

questions.question: Why should a service validate its configuration at startup and exit if something is missing?
questions.answer: A clear error at deploy time names the missing or bad setting immediately. Otherwise the service starts, looks healthy, and fails later on some request, far from the cause.
questions.explanation: Failing fast turns a confusing production incident into a failed deploy with an obvious message, which the pipeline can catch before users see anything.

questions.question: In a fresh clone, install the git hook so pre-commit runs on every commit.
questions.explanation: pre-commit install writes a hook script into .git/hooks. It is per clone, which is one reason CI must run the same checks.

questions.question: A GitHub Actions job has strategy.matrix.python-version set to ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]. What does that do?
choices: Runs the job once per listed Python version, in parallel
Runs the steps in random order
Retries failed steps three times
Installs three copies of every dependency in one job
questions.explanation: Each matrix value creates its own job. A library that claims to support 3.11 to 3.13 proves it by testing all three.

questions.question: Put these CI steps in a sensible order.
items: Install the project and dev dependencies
questions.explanation: Each step needs the previous one, and the fast static checks run before the slower test suite so obvious problems fail within seconds.
